title: Under the Neem Tree

sections.heading: Beginning
sections.content:
The morning sun rose over the Sahyadri hills and painted the sky in soft orange and pink. In a small village near Satara, the air smelled of wood smoke and fresh chai. Red soil paths connected the houses, and sugarcane fields stretched in every direction like a green ocean.

Sanika Jadhav walked quickly along the path to school, her two braids bouncing behind her. She carried her steel tiffin box in one hand and a set of colored pencils in the other. Her tiffin had bhakri with thecha and a small bowl of yogurt — her favorite lunch.

At the Zilla Parishad school, a blue-and-white painted building with four classrooms, children were already gathering under the big neem tree in the courtyard for morning assembly. Sanika spotted Rohit Kale standing quietly at the back of the line. Rohit was a thin boy with serious eyes who always seemed to be thinking about something far away. After school, while other children played lagori near the temple, Rohit walked home to help his father in the sugarcane fields.

After assembly, their teacher, Kavita Bai, stood before the class with a big smile.

"I have exciting news," she said. "During Bail Pola festival week, our taluka is holding a 'Best Village Display' competition. Each class must prepare a project that shows something special about our village."

The classroom buzzed with excitement. Sanika's hand shot up immediately. "Bai, can we draw pictures? I can make charts!"

"Of course, Sanika," Kavita Bai said warmly. "But a good project needs more than just pictures. It needs heart and truth."

Aniket Shinde, a tall boy who was the best at kabaddi, leaned toward Rohit and whispered loudly, "What will you do, Rohit? Draw a bullock?" A few children laughed.

Rohit looked down at his hands. They were rough from working in the fields. He said nothing, but his ears turned red.

Kavita Bai's eyes moved across the room. She noticed Rohit's silence, and her expression grew thoughtful.

sections.heading: Middle
sections.content:
Kavita Bai divided the class into groups of five. "Your project topic is 'Our Village's Farming Life,'" she announced. "Show the judges what makes our village's connection to the land special."

Sanika's group started working right away. She drew beautiful pictures of green fields and golden crops. Another girl, Priya, wrote neat labels in colorful markers. They made a big chart with borders of flowers and butterflies.

But after two days, Sanika sat back and frowned at their work. The charts were pretty, but something was missing. They looked like pictures from a textbook — not like their real village at all.

"It doesn't feel alive," Sanika told Priya. "It could be any village."

That afternoon, Sanika noticed Rohit sitting alone under the neem tree during the midday meal. Beside him on the ground sat a small piece of dried sugarcane stalk, a handful of jowar grains in a cloth, and two tiny wooden bullocks carved so carefully that you could see the curves of their horns.

"Rohit, what are those?" Sanika asked, sitting down next to him.

"My ajoba — my grandfather — carved these," Rohit said quietly, touching the little bullocks. "He makes them every year before Bail Pola. This one is Shiva and this one is Ganya — like our real bullocks."

"They are beautiful!" Sanika picked one up gently. "And what are the grains for?"

Rohit's eyes brightened. "These are jowar grains from our last harvest. If you hold them close, they still smell like the field after rain. My father says the red soil here gives the jowar its sweetness."

Sanika stared at him. "Rohit, you know so much about farming! You should join our group."

Rohit shook his head slowly. "Children will laugh. They say I only know about mud and bullocks."

"Then let them laugh," Sanika said firmly. "Mud and bullocks are what our village is built on. Bai said the project needs heart and truth. You have both."

Rohit hesitated for a long moment. Then, slowly, he nodded.

Over the next week, everything changed. Rohit brought real items from the farm — the sugarcane stalk, jowar and soybean seeds, a piece of red laterite soil in a clay pot, and his grandfather's carved bullocks. He explained how farmers plant soybean when the monsoon arrives. He told them how sugarcane grows tall over many months. And he described why Bail Pola is the most important day for farming families.

"On Pola, we thank Shiva and Ganya for their hard work," Rohit said, his voice growing stronger. "We wash them, paint their horns with bright colors, put bead necklaces around their necks, and feed them puran poli."

Sanika painted each scene — bullocks decorated with colorful beads, farmers walking behind their ploughs, rain falling on fresh green fields. Her drawings now had real stories behind them.

Other children wanted to help too. Priya brought her mother's thecha recipe written on a card. Aniket — the same boy who had teased Rohit — brought a photograph of decorated bullocks from last year's Pola. He placed it on the display without saying anything, but he looked at Rohit and gave a small nod.

"I didn't know all that about Pola," Aniket admitted quietly. "My family has buffaloes for milk, not bullocks for the field. It's different."

"Every family's work matters," Rohit said simply.

Kavita Bai watched from her desk and smiled.

sections.heading: End
sections.content:
The day of the taluka competition arrived. Judges from the Block Education Office came to the school. When they reached Sanika and Rohit's class, they stopped.

The display table was covered with a clean white cloth. Real jowar grains and soybean seeds sat in small clay bowls. The sugarcane stalk stood upright, tied with a ribbon. The tiny carved bullocks looked as though they might walk away at any moment. And behind it all, Sanika's paintings told the heartfelt story of a farming year — from the first monsoon shower to the Bail Pola celebration.

Rohit stood in front of the display. His hands trembled slightly, but when he picked up the jowar grains and held them out, his voice was steady.

"This is our village," he said. "My family grows sugarcane and soybean on our small plot. My father drives the bullock cart to the fields before sunrise. My mother tends the kitchen garden — tomatoes, mirchi, and shepu. These bullocks are Shiva and Ganya." He touched the wooden toys gently. "On Bail Pola, we feed them puran poli before we eat any ourselves, because they work the hardest."

Sanika stepped forward and pointed to her illustrations. "Rohit taught us that farming is not just work — it is a way of life."

One of the judges, a woman with kind eyes, picked up the carved bullock and examined it closely. "This is not just a project," she said. "This is your village, alive on this table."

That afternoon, the results were announced under the neem tree. Sanika and Rohit's class won second prize — a set of thirty books for the school library. The children cheered so loudly that birds flew out of the neem branches. Priya immediately asked Kavita Bai if there were any books about cooking in the set, and everyone laughed.

Aniket ran up to Rohit. "Next time, you must tell us more stories about the farm. Maybe I can bring something about our dairy buffaloes too."

Rohit smiled — a real, wide smile.

The next morning, the children crowded around the new books before class even started, arguing happily over who would read what first. Kavita Bai had to clap three times to get them back to their seats.

Three days later, Bail Pola arrived. Rohit's family woke before dawn. They bathed Shiva and Ganya in the river, painted their horns bright red and yellow, and hung garlands of colorful beads around their thick necks. Rohit fed them puran poli from his own hands. Ganya tried to eat the garland too, and Rohit's ajoba laughed so hard he had to sit down on a rock.

The whole village gathered for the procession. Dhol-tasha drums echoed through the valley. Sanika joined Rohit's family, walking proudly beside the decorated bullocks.

Afterward, they sat under the neem tree at Rohit's house, eating puran poli and laughing together. Kavita Bai visited and sat down on the stone bench.

"Remember this, children," she said. "No knowledge is small. The child who knows the earth knows the world."

Rohit looked at Sanika, and Sanika looked back at him. They didn't need to say anything. The neem tree spread its branches wide above them, and in the distance, the hills turned purple in the fading light.

characters.name: Sanika Jadhav
characters.role: A creative and kind 9-year-old girl who loves drawing and brings Rohit into her project group, recognizing the value of his knowledge.

characters.name: Rohit Kale
characters.role: A quiet, observant 10-year-old boy from a farming family who discovers his deep knowledge of farming life is a valuable gift.

characters.name: Kavita Bai
characters.role: The warm and wise teacher at the Zilla Parishad school who encourages every child to contribute their unique strengths.

characters.name: Aniket Shinde
characters.role: A sporty and mischievous classmate who initially teases Rohit but learns to appreciate and respect his knowledge.

vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Paused before doing something because of feeling unsure or nervous.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: The whole village gathered for the procession.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: A group of people walking together in a line to celebrate something special.

vocabulary_words.simple_definition: A type of reddish soil found in warm, tropical areas.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: Sanika stepped forward and pointed to her illustrations.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: A drawing or picture made to explain or decorate something.

vocabulary_words.context_sentence: Sanika's paintings told the heartfelt story of a farming year — from the first monsoon shower to the Bail Pola celebration.
vocabulary_words.simple_definition: Showing deep, honest, and sincere feelings.

moral_lesson: Working together and respecting every person's contribution — no matter how small — helps the whole community succeed. True friendship means lifting others up rather than competing against them. No knowledge is small; every person's life experience is valuable and worth sharing.
revisions_made: Fixed the 'heartfelt' vocabulary entry: inserted the word 'heartfelt' into the actual story text in the End section ('Sanika's paintings told the heartfelt story of a farming year') so the context sentence now matches the narrative, resolving the classroom-use disconnect.

Split the long compound sentence in the Middle section ('He explained to the group how farmers plant soybean when the monsoon arrives, how sugarcane grows tall over many months, and why Bail Pola is the most important day for farming families') into three shorter sentences for better ESL accessibility.

Added two humorous moments: (1) Priya asking if there are cooking books in the prize set, making everyone laugh; (2) Ganya the bullock trying to eat the garland during Bail Pola, causing Rohit's ajoba to laugh so hard he sits down. These lighten the earnest tone and engage reluctant readers.
Added a transition sentence about the children excitedly crowding around the new library books the next morning, reinforcing the tangible reward of collaboration before the Bail Pola scene.
